R004_credit.caption:
Your boss presented your work, and nobody even knew it was yours. 👀

You stayed late on it.
You fixed the numbers.
You built every slide.

Then in the meeting it became "the plan I put together."

In healthy teams, credit travels with the work.
In toxic workplaces, it travels up.

So put your name on it before the meeting. Send the final version yourself: "Sharing the final deck I built. Happy to walk everyone through it."
That's not bragging. It's a paper trail.

Has a toxic boss ever taken credit for YOUR work? 👇

Send this to the coworker who does the work behind the scenes.

C002_rules.caption:
When the rules only apply to you, it's not in your head. 👀

You're late once. Written warning.
They're late every week. A laugh and a "no worries."
Same policy. Different person.

Uneven rules aren't random.
They show you who's protected, and who isn't.

In healthy workplaces, the standard is the standard.
In toxic ones, it depends on who you are.

Don't argue "but they did it too" in the moment. Ask for the standard in writing: "So I meet expectations, could you confirm the policy?" Calm, neutral, and now it's on the record for everyone.

Has your workplace ever had one rulebook for you and another for the favorite? 👇

Save this for the next time the rules change, and send it to the coworker who's noticed it too.

R006_sickday.caption:
Calling in sick shouldn't feel like a court case. 👀

You wake up with a fever.
You send the message.
Then your boss asks if you're "REALLY" sick.

So you start explaining symptoms like you're on trial.

In healthy workplaces, a sick day is just a sick day.
In toxic ones, you have to earn it.

Next time, keep it short: "I'm unwell and won't be in today. I'll update you tomorrow."
That's not rude. It's enough.

Has a bad boss ever made YOU feel guilty for being sick? 👇

Send this to the coworker who works through every cold.

R007_notice.caption:
You owe them two weeks' notice. They can end it in one meeting. 👀

You give them your weekends.
You cover the extra shifts.
You stay because you're loyal.

Then a 15-minute "org update" shows up on the calendar with no agenda.

In healthy workplaces, loyalty goes both ways.
In toxic work culture, it only goes up.

So keep a quiet backup plan while things are calm: update your resume this week, write down three wins this month, and message one old coworker today.
That's not disloyal. It's being prepared.

Would YOU still give two weeks' notice after seeing a layoff like that? 👇

Send this to the coworker who survived the last layoff.
